people.name: Macrianus the Elder
people.summary: A rich and lame officer in charge of Valerian's finances and supplies in the east (procurator arcae et praepositus annonae), Macrianus took control of the remnants of the army after Valerian's capture in 260 and, judging himself too old and crippled, had his sons Macrianus and Quietus proclaimed emperors. Dionysius of Alexandria blames him for Valerian's persecution. He marched west with the younger Macrianus and was killed in 261.
people.death: killed with his army's defection in the Balkans, 261

people.name: Macrianus the Younger
people.summary: Proclaimed Augustus with his brother Quietus in 260 and recognised in Egypt and much of the east (coins at Antioch and Alexandria), he marched with his father against Gallienus and was killed when Aureolus' army defeated them in Illyricum or Thrace in 261.

people.name: Quietus
people.summary: Younger son of Macrianus, proclaimed Augustus in 260 and left in Syria with the prefect Ballista; after his family's defeat he was besieged at Emesa by Odaenathus and killed by the townspeople in late 261.

people.name: Ballista
people.summary: Praetorian prefect under Valerian and the Macriani, Ballista (called Callistus by Zonaras and Syncellus) defeated the Persians in Cilicia in 260, capturing part of Shapur's harem, and engineered the proclamation of Macrianus' sons. He was killed with Quietus at Emesa in 261; the Historia Augusta invents a later usurpation.

people.name: Sabinus Julianus
people.summary: Governor (corrector) in northern Italy or Pannonia who claimed the purple on hearing of Numerian's death in 284 and struck coins at Siscia; Carinus defeated and killed him near Verona early in 285.

people.name: Rufius Volusianus
people.summary: Senator with an exceptional career straddling five regimes: corrector of Italy (c. 281-289), proconsul of Africa (305-306), Maxentius' praetorian prefect who crushed Domitius Alexander (309/310), consul in 311 and, under Constantine, prefect of Rome (313-315) and consul again in 314. Ancestor of the great Ceionii Rufii of fourth-century Rome.

people.name: Dalmatius
people.summary: Son of Constantine's half-brother Flavius Dalmatius, educated at Narbo, he suppressed Calocaerus' revolt in Cyprus (334) and was made Caesar on 18 September 335 with Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea. He was murdered by the soldiers in the purge of summer 337, which removed the collateral line from the succession.

people.name: Hannibalianus

roles.t: King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples

people.summary: Brother of the Caesar Dalmatius and husband of Constantine's daughter Constantina, Hannibalianus was appointed in 335 "King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples" (rex regum et Ponticarum gentium), apparently intended to rule Armenia after a Persian war; his unique coins show the Euphrates reclining. He was murdered in 337.

people.name: Constantina
people.summary: Elder daughter of Constantine and Fausta, styled Augusta by her father, she married her cousin Hannibalianus (335) and, after his murder, Constantius Gallus (351). In 350 she persuaded the old general Vetranio to take the purple against Magnentius. Ammianus portrays her as a "Megaera" goading Gallus to cruelty; she died of fever in Bithynia in 354 on her way to plead with Constantius, and was buried in her mausoleum on the Via Nomentana.
people.death: fever at Caeni Gallicani in Bithynia, 354

people.name: Gennobaudes
people.summary: Frankish king on the lower Rhine who submitted to Maximian about 288 and, according to the panegyrist, received his kingdom back as a gift from the emperor, the first named Frankish ruler to become a Roman client.

people.name: Bahram II
people.summary: Sasanian King of Kings 274-293, grandson of Shapur I, who ruled under the influence of the Zoroastrian high priest Kirdir (Kartir), persecuting Manichaeans, Christians and Jews. Faced with Carus' invasion (283) and his brother Hormizd's revolt in Sakastan, he made peace with Diocletian in 287. His rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Sar Mashhad show him with his family and killing lions.

people.name: Arsaces II
people.summary: Arsacid king of Armenia c. 350-368, married first to the Roman Olympias (fiancée of Constans) and then to Pharantzem; caught between Rome and Persia, he was abandoned by the treaty of 363, lured to Persia by Shapur II, blinded and imprisoned in the Castle of Oblivion, where Armenian tradition says he killed himself.

people.name: Pap
people.summary: Son of Arsaces II and Pharantzem, Pap escaped from besieged Artogerassa and was restored to the Armenian throne by Valens (c. 370); the battle of Bagavan secured him, but his independence and contacts with Persia led Valens to have him murdered at a banquet given by the dux Traianus in 374 or 375.

people.name: Arbitio
people.summary: A soldier who rose from the ranks to magister equitum (351-361) and consul (355), Arbitio was a feared intriguer at Constantius' court who helped ruin Ursicinus and Silvanus. He sat on Julian's commission at Chalcedon, and in 366, called out of retirement, persuaded Procopius' troops to desert by appealing to them as their old commander.

people.name: Barbatio
people.summary: Commander of Gallus' guard who arrested his master in 354, then magister peditum (355-359); he failed to cooperate with Julian in 357 and was defeated by the Alamanni near Augst. In 359 he and his wife Assyria were executed after she wrote him a letter hoping he would become emperor, an episode Ammianus links to an omen of bees swarming in his house.

people.name: Nevitta
people.summary: A German (perhaps Frankish) officer, Nevitta led one of Julian's columns through Raetia in 361, was made magister equitum and consul for 362, sat on the Chalcedon tribunal, and commanded in the Persian campaign; Ammianus calls him uncouth and cruel, and criticises Julian for giving barbarians the consulship.

people.name: Salutius
people.summary: Gallic pagan and friend of Julian, praetorian prefect of the East 361-367, Salutius presided over the Chalcedon trials and was twice offered the throne, after Julian's death in 363 and after Jovian's in 364, refusing both on grounds of age; he negotiated the treaty of 363. He is perhaps the Sallustius who wrote the Neoplatonic catechism On the Gods and the Cosmos.

people.name: Jovinus
people.summary: Magister equitum in Gaul from 361 under Julian, Jovian and Valentinian I, consul in 367, Jovinus defeated the Alamannic invaders of 366 at Scarponna and Catalauni; a Christian, he built the church of St Agricola at Reims, where his sarcophagus with a lion hunt is preserved.

people.name: Julius
people.summary: Magister militum per Orientem 371-378, Julius ordered the massacre of Gothic youths and hostages in the eastern provinces after Adrianople, a deed Ammianus calls salutary and Zosimus describes in detail.

people.name: Merobaudes
people.summary: Frankish general, magister peditum in the west from 375 to 388 and consul in 377 and 383, Merobaudes engineered the proclamation of Valentinian II in 375 and dominated Gratian's government; he joined Magnus Maximus after Gratian's fall and died, by suicide or murder, during or after the war of 388.

people.name: Promotus
people.summary: Magister peditum in Thrace who destroyed Odotheus' Greuthungi on the Danube in 386, commanded cavalry against Maximus in 388 and was consul in 389; quarrelling with the prefect Rufinus, he was sent to Thrace and killed in a barbarian ambush in 391, which Zosimus attributes to Rufinus' intrigue. Stilicho buried him and avenged him on the Bastarnae.
people.death: killed in an ambush in Thrace, 391

people.name: Vadomarius
people.summary: Alamannic king opposite Augst and brother of Gundomad, Vadomarius made a treaty with Constantius in 354 and, secretly encouraged by him, raided Raetia in 361; Julian had him seized at a dinner and sent to Spain. He later served Rome as dux of Phoenicia, besieged Nicaea for Valens against Procopius (365), and fought the Persians in Armenia (371).

people.name: Macrianus
people.summary: King of the Bucinobantes opposite Mainz, the most formidable Alamannic leader of the 370s; Valentinian tried to kidnap him in 372 but made a treaty with him in boats on the Rhine in 374. He remained a loyal ally until killed fighting the Frankish king Mallobaudes.

people.name: Mavia
people.summary: Arab queen, probably of the Tanukh federation, who after her husband's death c. 375 led raids into Phoenicia, Palestine and Egypt, defeating Roman forces, then made peace on condition that the monk Moses be made bishop of her people. Her daughter married the magister Victor, and her cavalry helped defend Constantinople in 378. An inscription at Anasartha may commemorate her.

people.name: Cynegius
people.summary: Spanish Christian and close associate of Theodosius, praetorian prefect of the East 384-388 and consul 388, Cynegius toured Egypt and Syria closing temples and encouraging their destruction, earning Libanius' hostility (Oration 30). He died in office at Constantinople in March 388; his widow Acanthia carried his body back to Spain.

people.name: Praetextatus
people.summary: Leading pagan senator, priest of many cults (pontifex, augur, initiate of Eleusis, Mithraic pater patrum, hierophant of Hecate), proconsul of Achaea (362-364), prefect of Rome (367-368) and praetorian prefect (384). Jerome reports him joking to Pope Damasus: "Make me bishop of Rome and I will become a Christian at once." His funerary monument with his wife Paulina (CIL VI 1779) is a manifesto of late paganism; Macrobius made him host of the Saturnalia.
people.death: died before taking up the consulship of 385

people.name: Nicomachus Flavianus
people.summary: Senator, historian (his lost Annales were dedicated to Theodosius) and friend of Symmachus, praetorian prefect of Italy under Theodosius (390-392) and again under Eugenius, whose pagan revival he led; consul 394. After the Frigidus he committed suicide; his memory was rehabilitated in 431. Many scholars think his Annales underlie the Latin historical tradition of Ammianus and the Historia Augusta.
people.death: suicide after the battle of the Frigidus, September 394

people.name: Junius Bassus
people.summary: Son of the consul of 331, Junius Bassus was prefect of Rome when he died on 25 August 359 aged 42, having been baptised shortly before; his sarcophagus from St Peter's, with its double register of Old and New Testament scenes, is the finest example of fourth-century Christian sculpture.

people.name: Optatian
people.summary: Poet, probably African, exiled for an unknown offence, who won Constantine's pardon with a book of figured poems in which highlighted letters form images and secondary verses; Constantine replied in a surviving letter. He became prefect of Rome in 329 and 333.

people.name: Porphyry
people.summary: Born Malchus at Tyre, student of Longinus at Athens and from 263 of Plotinus in Rome, Porphyry edited Plotinus' Enneads with a Life of the master, wrote the Isagoge (the standard logic primer for a millennium), On Abstinence from animal food, Letter to Marcella, the Philosophy from Oracles and the fifteen books Against the Christians, the most learned ancient attack on Christianity, burned by imperial order in 448.

people.name: Iamblichus
people.summary: Syrian philosopher, possibly of the Emesene royal line, pupil of Porphyry, who taught at Apamea and turned Neoplatonism towards theurgy, defending ritual in On the Mysteries against Porphyry and writing a Pythagorean encyclopedia (On the Pythagorean Life). Through Aedesius, Maximus of Ephesus and Sallustius his system became the intellectual basis of Julian's pagan restoration.

people.name: Themistius
people.summary: Paphlagonian philosopher and paraphrast of Aristotle who taught at Constantinople, was adlected to the Senate by Constantius (355) and served six emperors as official orator, arguing for religious toleration (Or. 5 to Jovian) and, after Adrianople, for peace with the Goths (Or. 16). Theodosius made him prefect of Constantinople in 384 and tutor of Arcadius. His Aristotle paraphrases were read in Arabic and Hebrew.

people.name: Prohaeresius
people.summary: Armenian-born Christian sophist who held the leading chair of rhetoric at Athens, teaching Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus; Rome set up his statue inscribed "Queen of Cities to the King of Eloquence". He resigned in 362 rather than accept Julian's exemption from the school law.

people.name: Marius Victorinus
people.summary: African rhetor at Rome honoured with a statue in Trajan's Forum, translator of Porphyry's Isagoge and Neoplatonic texts into Latin, whose late conversion (c. 355), professed publicly in church, Augustine describes as a model for his own. As a Christian he wrote dense Neoplatonic treatises against the Arians and the first Latin commentaries on Paul; he resigned his chair under Julian's school law.

people.name: Ausonius
people.summary: Rhetor of Bordeaux for thirty years, summoned c. 364 to tutor Gratian at Trier, Ausonius rose with his pupil to the praetorian prefecture of Gaul (377-379) and the consulship of 379, filling offices with his family. His varied poems include the Mosella, the Parentalia on his relatives, the Professores of Bordeaux and the Ordo urbium nobilium; he corresponded with his pupil Paulinus of Nola, who renounced poetry for asceticism.

people.name: Aurelius Victor
people.summary: African of humble rural origin who rose through the imperial bureaucracy, Aurelius Victor wrote the Liber de Caesaribus (361), a moralising history of emperors from Augustus to Constantius; Julian made him consular of Pannonia Secunda and Theodosius prefect of Rome (389).

people.name: Eutropius
people.summary: Bureaucrat who served under Julian in Persia (363) and as magister memoriae under Valens, for whom he wrote the Breviarium ab urbe condita (c. 369), a lucid ten-book survey of Roman history; often identified with the Eutropius who was proconsul of Asia (371-372) and praetorian prefect of Illyricum (380-381), and perhaps consul in 387.

people.name: Arnobius
people.summary: Rhetor at Sicca Veneria in Africa Proconsularis and teacher of Lactantius, who wrote the seven books Adversus Nationes around 300 to convince his bishop of his conversion; vivid and sarcastic, they preserve much about pagan myth and ritual and show an idiosyncratic theology little shaped by Scripture.

people.name: Firmicus Maternus
people.summary: Sicilian of senatorial rank, author of the Mathesis (c. 335), the most complete Latin astrological manual, which includes a horoscope probably of Ceionius Rufius Albinus; after conversion he wrote On the Error of Profane Religions (c. 346), urging Constantius and Constans to destroy paganism by force.

people.name: Proba
people.summary: Roman aristocrat, wife of Clodius Celsinus Adelphius (prefect of Rome 351) and ancestor of the Anicii, who wrote a lost epic on the war of Constantius and Magnentius and the surviving Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi, retelling Genesis and the Gospels in Virgil's own lines.
